History:
- 28-year-old female presents with a new onset headache, started yesterday mid-morning.
- Headache located on the left side, at the back of the head.
- Described as intense, throbbing pain; rated 8/10 in severity.
- Gradually built up over a short period.
- No prior similar episodes; headaches are unusual for her.
- No associated symptoms: no nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, limb weakness, tingling, numbness, fever, chills, sweats, rash, or neck stiffness.
- No relation to time of day, activity, or body position.
- Able to eat, drink, and sleep normally; but finds it hard to do normal activities and work.
- No recent stress, dietary, or lifestyle changes reported.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic illnesses reported.
- No previous hospitalizations reported.
- No regular medications.
- Took Nurofen (Ibuprofen; dose/route/frequency not documented) yesterday, with minimal effect.
- No allergies reported.
- No asthma or stomach problems.
- Family history: Mother has hypertension and migraines.
- No smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use.

Physical Examination:
- No physical exam findings reported (virtual consult).
- No reported fever, rash, neurological deficits, visual changes, or altered consciousness.
- Alert and communicative; able to answer questions appropriately.

Impression:
- New onset unilateral headache, likely primary headache etiology (migraine/tension type not specified), no red flag symptoms identified.

Management Plan:
- Advise trial of a stronger pain reliever, different from Ibuprofen, taken regularly with food (medication name/dose not specified).
- Paracetamol recommended as an additional option.
- Emphasis on rest and adequate hydration.
- If headache worsens or if new symptoms develop (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, recurrent episodes), instructed to seek further medical attention promptly.

Patient Summary:
- 28-year-old woman with a new, severe left-sided headache without concerning associated symptoms; no prior headache history.
- No signs of serious underlying disease identified at this time.
- Conservative management with analgesia, hydration, and close monitoring advised.

Key Takeaways:
- Take the prescribed pain relief and Paracetamol as instructed, with food.
- Rest and stay hydrated.
- Seek urgent care if symptoms worsen, persist beyond 1–2 days, or new symptoms (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness) develop.

Next Steps:
- Monitor symptoms over the next 1–2 days.
- If not improving or if red flag symptoms appear, contact physician or seek urgent review.
- If recurring headaches develop, follow-up for further evaluation may be necessary.
